title: 1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password
content:
Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up.
Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials.
The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents, accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand.
1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service.
“Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post. “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.”
Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts.
This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not.
Bankers interviewed by the outlet described the situation as “horrifying,” and a Chase spokesperson interviewed by Axios additionally told the outlet that customers “should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone.”

report.summary: 1Password for Agents lets AI agents log into user accounts via a confirmed digital key, so the agent never sees the password.
report.background: Consumers are increasingly delegating online tasks to AI agents, including actions that require logging into personal accounts. The common shortcut is to hand over passwords or secrets directly, which creates copies of sensitive credentials in places users cannot control. Security providers are now trying to catch up by building identity and consent layers specifically for agentic activity. The launch comes as U.S. banks report detecting automated agent activity inside customer accounts and say they often cannot tell whether it was authorized by the user. A Chase spokesperson reiterated that customers should not share usernames and passwords with anyone, underscoring the gap between agent adoption and credential-security practices.
key_points: 1Password for Agents works as a broker: the agent presents a unique digital key to 1Password, the user receives an alert and confirms the login, and 1Password fills in the credentials on the agent’s behalf. The agent completes the task without ever receiving the password or secret.

The service is designed to be agent-agnostic. 1Password says users can choose from agents including Anthropic’s Claude Duet, OpenAI’s Dots and ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, and Town, with more integrations planned.

The security rationale is delegation without credential exposure. Instead of saving a password copy for an agent to reuse, 1Password keeps the secret inside the password manager and gives the user a confirmation point for each login attempt.

The launch lands amid rising institutional concern. Banks are detecting agentic activity in customer accounts but often cannot distinguish authorized agent actions from unauthorized ones, prompting warnings from banks about sharing credentials.
report.impact: The move signals that agent security is shifting from password sharing toward delegated identity, consent, and auditability. For the AI industry, it creates a potential trust layer for agent commerce and personal automation, but it also raises questions about standards, interoperability, and liability when an agent acts wrongly. Developers will need to design agents around scoped authorization, user approval flows, and logs rather than stored credentials. For regular users, the benefit is safer delegation without exposing passwords, though confirmation fatigue and social-engineering risks remain. Banks and online services may eventually need to recognize verified agent identities, not just human logins.
report.tools: Watch 1Password for Agents as the vendor offering; OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693) for scoped delegated access; SPIFFE/SPIRE, an open-source workload identity framework; WebAuthn/passkeys for phishing-resistant user approval; and OpenID AuthZEN for authorization APIs. Developers can prototype agent consent screens, per-task scopes, and audit logs around these standards.
